context.heading: Faith without a mask
context.body: Timothy's faith is anypokritos ("sincere"), literally "un-hypocritical"; a hypokritēs was a stage actor behind a mask. His Jewish mother and grandmother taught him the Scriptures from childhood, though his father was Greek (2 Timothy 3:15; Acts 16:1). Faith passed on at home proved real enough to carry into a new generation.

context.heading: Not fear but cowardice
context.body: Deilia is not ordinary fear but cowardice, the shrinking back that abandons duty under pressure. In its place God gives power, love and sōphronismos, a sound, disciplined mind that thinks clearly under stress. With Paul in chains and Christians under suspicion in Nero's Rome, Timothy had real reasons to keep his head down.

context.heading: The man who went looking
context.body: While Phygelus, Hermogenes and others in Asia deserted Paul (v. 15), Onesiphorus "searched diligently" until he found him in Rome. Tracking down one prisoner in a city of perhaps a million, and being seen with him, carried real risk. Paul says he often refreshed him (anapsychō, "to let breathe again," like cool air after heat).

theology.title: Grace planned before time
theology.body: God saved us "not because of our works, but by His own purpose and by the grace He granted us in Christ Jesus before time began" (v. 9). Salvation was not a backup plan after the fall but God's purpose from eternity (Ephesians 1:4). Because it rests on His purpose, it does not wobble with our performance.

theology.title: Death put out of action
theology.body: Christ "has abolished death" (v. 10). The verb katargeō means to render powerless, to put out of action. Believers still die, but for a man awaiting execution, death had lost its final word, as Isaiah promised when he said God would swallow up death forever (Isaiah 25:8).

application.title: Courage starts with memory
application.body: Timothy's problem was not lack of gifting but timidity. Paul doesn't tell him to try harder to feel brave; he reminds him what God has already given.
application.question: Where are you staying quiet about Jesus to avoid a moment of awkwardness?

application.title: Be the one who shows up
application.body: When others distanced themselves from Paul, Onesiphorus went looking for him and was not ashamed of his chains. Loyalty is tested most when being associated with someone costs you something.
application.question: Who in your life is going through something isolating that you have quietly stepped back from?

application.title: Faith at the kitchen table
application.body: Timothy's faith came through his grandmother and mother, not a famous preacher. Lasting discipleship often happens in ordinary homes, through faith that is real when no one else is watching.
application.question: What are the people in your home learning about God from how you act when you are tired or stressed?

context.heading: Soldiers without side jobs
context.body: Roman legionaries served twenty years or more, and for most of this era they could not legally marry while enlisted. Emplekō ("entangle") is the word for getting caught, as in a net. Paul is not calling ordinary life bad; his point is that a soldier on active duty cannot be pulled in two directions and still please his commander.

context.heading: No crown for cheaters
context.body: Athleō ("compete") gives us "athlete." At Olympia, competitors swore before a statue of Zeus that they had trained for ten months and would keep the rules. A rule-breaker was fined or disqualified, however fast he ran. Paul says the Christian life has a finish line and a right way to run toward it.

context.heading: Teaching that spreads like gangrene
context.body: Gangraina is a medical term for a spreading infection that eats healthy flesh. Hymenaeus and Philetus claimed the resurrection had already happened (v. 18), probably meaning a purely spiritual one. Denying the future bodily resurrection was not a minor quibble; it was already destroying the faith of some.

theology.title: He remains faithful
theology.body: The saying in verses 11–13 moves in pairs: dying and living with Christ, enduring and reigning. Then it turns: "if we are faithless, He remains faithful, for He cannot deny Himself." God's faithfulness rests on His unchanging character (Numbers 23:19), though the warning "if we deny Him, He will also deny us" stands right beside it.

theology.title: The Lord knows His own
theology.body: God's foundation bears a seal with two inscriptions (v. 19). "The Lord knows those who are His" quotes Numbers 16:5, from Korah's rebellion, when God distinguished true leaders from false. The call to turn from wickedness echoes the same story (Numbers 16:26). God sees through religious disguise and will make plain who belongs to Him.

application.title: Who are you training?
application.body: Verse 2 spans four generations: Paul, Timothy, faithful people, and others after them. Faith that stops with you has not finished its job.
application.question: Who is one person you are deliberately passing your faith on to right now?

application.title: Stop trying to win
application.body: Paul tells Timothy to avoid foolish controversies and correct opponents gently, because God may grant them repentance. Comment-section debates rarely change anyone, and the Lord's servant "must not be quarrelsome."
application.question: Which argument do you care more about winning than about the other person coming to the truth?

application.title: Ready for any use
application.body: In a large house some vessels are kept for honorable use and others for common use. What you watch, scroll and repeat shapes what kind of vessel you are when God hands you a good work.
application.question: What would you need to stop consuming to be ready for the next good work God puts in front of you?

context.heading: Savage times
context.body: Chalepos means hard or dangerous; Matthew uses it of two demon-possessed men so fierce no one could pass (Matthew 8:28). In the New Testament "the last days" usually means the whole era between Jesus' first and second comings (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2). Paul tells Timothy to avoid such people now (v. 5), so he is describing Timothy's present as well as the future.

context.heading: Jannes and Jambres
context.body: The Old Testament does not name Pharaoh's magicians who opposed Moses (Exodus 7:11, 22), but Jewish tradition did, calling them Jannes and Jambres. Paul draws on that familiar tradition the way a preacher might mention a well-known story. Their imitation of God's power impressed for a while, but their folly became plain (Exodus 8:18–19).

context.heading: Breathed out by God
context.body: Theopneustos ("God-breathed") is first found here in surviving Greek, and Paul may have coined it. It means Scripture is not merely inspiring but breathed out by God, as His breath gave life to Adam (Genesis 2:7) and His word made the heavens (Psalm 33:6). For Timothy, "Scripture" meant mainly the Old Testament, though Peter already places Paul's letters alongside it (2 Peter 3:16).

theology.title: God has spoken enough
theology.body: Because Scripture is breathed out by God, it carries His authority to teach, rebuke, correct and train (v. 16). Its goal is that the person of God may be artios ("complete"), "fully equipped for every good work" (v. 17). God has not left His people guessing; He has spoken sufficiently for a faithful life.

theology.title: Scripture leads to Christ
theology.body: The writings Timothy knew from infancy "are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus" (v. 15). Jesus said the same: the Scriptures testify about Him (Luke 24:27; John 5:39). The whole Old Testament story bends toward Christ.

theology.title: Rescue through, not around
theology.body: Paul recalls Antioch, Iconium and Lystra, where he was driven out and stoned (Acts 13–14), "yet the Lord rescued me from all of them" (v. 11). Lystra was Timothy's hometown (Acts 16:1), so he may have seen it. God's rescue did not spare Paul from suffering; it carried him through it.

application.title: Godliness as a costume
application.body: Paul describes people with "a form of godliness" who deny its power. You can attend, post verses and know the vocabulary while nothing inside is changing.
application.question: Where does your faith look better from the outside than it is on the inside?

application.title: The default settings
application.body: Paul's list starts with loving self and money and ends with loving pleasure rather than God. These are not exotic sins; they are the default settings of a consumer culture, and church people are not immune.
application.question: Which item on that list best describes how you spent your last free evening?

application.title: Equipped, not just informed
application.body: Paul says Scripture equips people for every good work. Reading a chapter can feel finished once you understand it, but the aim is to come away ready to act.
application.question: What specific good work is today's reading equipping you to do before tomorrow?

context.heading: Ears that itch
context.body: Knēthō pictures ears that itch to be scratched, wanting the pleasant sensation of hearing what they already like. Greco-Roman cities had plenty of traveling speakers who drew crowds by entertaining them. Paul warns that people will "gather around themselves" (episōreuō, "heap up") teachers who suit their desires.

context.heading: Books in a prison cell
context.body: Along with his cloak, Paul asks for his scrolls and "especially the parchments" (membrana), writing material made from animal skin. They may have been notebooks, legal papers or copies of Scripture; no one knows. With winter coming (v. 21) and death near, Paul still wanted to read and study.

context.heading: Alone at the first defense
context.body: Apologia was a formal defense in court, the word behind "apologetics." At Paul's preliminary hearing no one stood with him, yet he used the moment to proclaim the gospel to Gentile hearers (v. 17). "Delivered from the mouth of the lion" is probably a figure for escaping immediate death, echoing Psalm 22:21.

theology.title: The righteous Judge
theology.body: Paul charges Timothy before Christ Jesus, "who will judge the living and the dead" (v. 1), words later echoed in the Apostles' Creed. The same Lord is "the righteous Judge" who awards a crown to all who long for His appearing (v. 8). A Roman court would soon judge Paul, but he looked past it to the court that mattered.

theology.title: The Lord stood by me
theology.body: When everyone deserted him, "the Lord stood by me and strengthened me" (v. 17). This echoes God's promise never to leave His people (Deuteronomy 31:6; Hebrews 13:5) and Jesus standing by Paul in an earlier crisis (Acts 23:11). God's presence is often most real when human support disappears.

application.title: Out of season
application.body: Timothy is to be ready "in season and out of season," when the word is welcome and when it isn't. Speaking truth only when it is convenient is not courage; it is timing.
application.question: What true thing are you waiting for a more comfortable moment to say?

application.title: Asking for Mark
application.body: Mark had once deserted Paul, and the two parted sharply over it (Acts 15:37–39). Now Paul asks for him by name because he is "useful to me in the ministry." Paul did not let one failure define a person forever.
application.question: Who have you written off because of one failure that you might need to invite back?

application.title: Finish, don't just start
application.body: Paul could say he had finished the race, while Demas deserted him "in his love of this world." Faithfulness is measured at the finish, not at the start.
application.question: What would need to change now for you to say you kept the faith at the end of your life?
